title: Joshua 10:28–43
context: This unit summarizes Joshua’s southern campaign city by city: Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir, with Horam of Gezer defeated when he comes to help Lachish. A repeated formula, struck with the edge of the sword, utterly destroyed, no one left, presents herem, the devoting of a city to destruction. The summary in 10:40–42 says this was done as the LORD commanded (compare Deuteronomy 7:1–2; 20:16–18) and credits the victories to the LORD fighting for Israel. Readers in both traditions find this language morally difficult and treat it as a unique judgment tied to the conquest, not a model for today. Later passages in Joshua and Judges describe Hebron and Debir being taken again (Joshua 15:13–17; Judges 1:10–13), which many readers take as a sign that the summary is stylized.

verses.text: Joshua took Makkedah on that day, and struck it with the edge of the sword, with its king. He utterly destroyed it and all the souls who were in it. He left no one remaining. He did to the king of Makkedah as he had done to the king of Jericho.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua takes Makkedah, striking it and its king and leaving no one. Arminian readers state the text plainly and acknowledge its moral weight, while noting that many read the formula as part of a stylized war report.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm God’s right to judge and read the act within the specific command of Deuteronomy 7:1–2. Shared ground: both traditions treat this as a unique judgment tied to the conquest of Canaan, not a model for any later people.

verses.text: Joshua passed from Makkedah, and all Israel with him, to Libnah, and fought against Libnah.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua moves from Makkedah to Libnah and fights against it. Arminian readers note the brisk, repetitive style of the campaign report, which moves quickly from city to city without describing each battle at length.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sequence as showing the LORD leading Israel step by step through the south. Both traditions acknowledge that the location of Libnah, like Makkedah, is debated and that the account focuses on the sequence rather than on geography.

verses.text: The LORD delivered it also, with its king, into the hand of Israel. He struck it with the edge of the sword, and all the souls who were in it. He left no one remaining in it. He did to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD gives Libnah and its king into Israel’s hand, and no one is left. Arminian readers note that the text credits the LORD first, keeping the focus on divine action rather than on Israel’s strength or skill.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see each city’s fall as one more fulfillment of God’s promise in 10:8 and 10:19. Shared ground: the formula repeats deliberately, presenting the whole campaign as the LORD’s work carried out through Israel’s army.

verses.text: Joshua passed from Libnah, and all Israel with him, to Lachish, and encamped against it, and fought against it.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua moves from Libnah to Lachish, besieges it, and fights. Arminian readers note that Lachish was one of the five coalition cities, so the campaign now reaches the home cities of the kings who attacked Gibeon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the advance on Lachish as God completing the judgment begun at Gibeon. Lachish is widely identified as an important city in the lowland, and both traditions read its siege as a turning point in the southern campaign.

verses.text: The LORD delivered Lachish into the hand of Israel. He took it on the second day, and struck it with the edge of the sword, with all the souls who were in it, according to all that he had done to Libnah.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD gives Lachish to Israel on the second day. Arminian readers note that this siege takes longer than the others, a detail suggesting a well-defended city and a report that does not treat every victory as instant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers again stress that the LORD delivers the city, even when the process takes time. Both traditions agree that the text’s realism about the second day sits alongside its claim that victory came from God.

verses.text: Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish; and Joshua struck him and his people, until he had left him no one remaining.
verses.arminianNotes: Horam of Gezer comes to help Lachish and is defeated. Arminian readers note that the text does not say Gezer itself was taken; later Joshua 16:10 says its Canaanites were not driven out, showing the summary’s limits.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Gezer remained outside Israel’s control until much later (1 Kings 9:16). Shared ground: the verse records a battle against Gezer’s king and army, and the wider book shows that not every city fell at once.

verses.text: Joshua passed from Lachish, and all Israel with him, to Eglon; and they encamped against it and fought against it.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel encamps against Eglon after Lachish falls. Arminian readers observe that the army keeps pressing on without returning to camp, and that Eglon’s own king was among those executed at Makkedah (10:23–26).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the steady march through the coalition’s cities as showing God’s thoroughness in judgment. Both traditions note that Eglon’s precise site remains a matter of discussion and that the text names it without further detail.

verses.text: They took it on that day, and struck it with the edge of the sword. He utterly destroyed all the souls who were in it that day, according to all that he had done to Lachish.
verses.arminianNotes: Eglon is taken that day and its people destroyed, as was done to Lachish. Arminian readers acknowledge the severity of the language and read it alongside the book’s other hints that summary statements can be stylized.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the destruction as God’s judgment on the Amorites, whose iniquity had reached its full measure (Genesis 15:16). Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as tied to this campaign alone and not as a pattern for believers.

verses.text: Joshua went up from Eglon, and all Israel with him, to Hebron; and they fought against it.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua goes up from Eglon to Hebron and fights against it. Arminian readers note the move from the lowland up into the hill country, where Hebron, another coalition city linked to Abraham’s story, is located.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note Hebron’s ties to the patriarchs (Genesis 23:2, 19) and see the campaign returning Israel to land promised to Abraham. Both traditions read the city’s capture within the story of God’s promises to the fathers.

verses.text: They took it, and struck it with the edge of the sword, with its king and all its cities, and all the souls who were in it. He left no one remaining, according to all that he had done to Eglon; but he utterly destroyed it, and all the souls who were in it.
verses.arminianNotes: Hebron, its king, and its towns are taken and devoted to destruction. Arminian readers note that its king had already died at Makkedah (10:23–26), and many see the reference here as a successor or as part of formulaic language.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Caleb later takes Hebron (Joshua 15:13–14), and some read this as a sign that Joshua’s summary covers repeated phases of conquest. Shared ground: both traditions read the account with attention to its summary style.

verses.text: Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to Debir, and fought against it.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua turns back to Debir and fights against it. Arminian readers note that Debir was not among the five coalition cities, so the campaign extends beyond the original alliance to the wider southern region.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the turn to Debir as the conquest reaching further into the land God promised. Both traditions acknowledge that Debir’s exact location is debated, and that the narrative’s interest is in the sequence of victories.

verses.text: He took it, with its king and all its cities. They struck them with the edge of the sword, and utterly destroyed all the souls who were in it. He left no one remaining. As he had done to Hebron, so he did to Debir, and to its king; as he had done also to Libnah, and to its king.
verses.arminianNotes: Debir and its towns are taken and devoted to destruction, as was done to Hebron and Libnah. Arminian readers note that Othniel later takes Debir again (Joshua 15:15–17), and see a stylized account of a longer process.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm that the destruction carries out the command given through Moses, while recognizing that the book itself reports later campaigns. Shared ground: both traditions read 10:39 as part of a summary rather than an exhaustive record.

verses.text: So Joshua struck all the land, the hill country, the South, the lowland, the slopes, and all their kings. He left no one remaining, but he utterly destroyed all that breathed, as the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua strikes the hill country, the South, the lowland, and the slopes, destroying all that breathed as the LORD commanded. Arminian readers state the command plainly and acknowledge that it remains deeply troubling to many readers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm that the text grounds the act in God’s command (Deuteronomy 20:16–17) and His justice. Shared ground: both traditions read this as a one-time judgment within redemptive history, never a warrant for violence today.

verses.text: Joshua struck them from Kadesh Barnea even to Gaza, and all the country of Goshen, even to Gibeon.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua strikes from Kadesh Barnea to Gaza and all the country of Goshen to Gibeon. Arminian readers note that this Goshen is a region in southern Canaan (compare 11:16; 15:51), not the Goshen in Egypt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the boundaries as marking the whole southern region now under Israel’s hand, from the desert edge to the coast and back toward Gibeon. Both traditions read the verse as a summary of territory, not a list of every battle.

verses.text: Joshua took all these kings and their land at one time because the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua takes all these kings and their land at one time, because the LORD fought for Israel. Arminian readers note that 11:18 says Joshua made war a long time, so “at one time” may refer to one campaign rather than one day.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the reason given: the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel, echoing 10:14. Shared ground: both traditions agree that the chapter’s victories are credited to God, and that the summary compresses events.

verses.text: Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp to Gilgal.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua and all Israel return to the camp at Gilgal. Arminian readers note that the chapter ends where Israel’s life in the land began, at the camp near the memorial stones set up after crossing the Jordan (4:19–20).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the return to Gilgal as a return to the place of covenant renewal (5:2–9), placing the campaign within Israel’s covenant life. Both traditions read this repeated line as closing the southern campaign account.
